title: AI You Didn't Choose — Module Quiz

items.q: Why does embedded AI need different scrutiny from an assistant you opened?
options: It uses weaker models
You may not know it is involved, never evaluated it, and it acts by default
It is always less accurate
items.explain: All three conditions that make deliberate use safer — awareness, evaluation, and acting only when asked — are absent.

items.q: For many people their main AI use is now:
options: A chatbot they open deliberately
Generated answers at the top of search results
Image generation
items.explain: And most have never called it AI use, which is exactly why it goes unchecked.

items.q: Why do defaults matter so much?
options: They are hard to change
Most people never change one, so the vendor's choice governs almost everyone
They cannot be changed on mobile
items.explain: "I did not turn this on" and "I agreed to this" are different statements.

items.q: Which word most reliably signals an AI feature without saying 'AI'?
options: Advanced
Smart
Premium
items.explain: Smart, suggested, auto, intelligent, magic and enhance are the vocabulary — usually beside a sparkle icon.

items.q: The most important question about an embedded feature:
options: Which model does it use?
Does my content leave the device, and where does it go?
What does it cost?
items.explain: That determines whether the paste test applies. On-device prediction and a cloud summariser are different propositions.

items.q: If you cannot determine where a feature sends your data:
options: Assume on-device, since that is now common
Assume cloud and third party
Assume it is not AI
items.explain: That is the assumption that keeps you safe if you turn out to be wrong.

items.q: A toggle labelled 'Show suggestions' most likely:
options: Stops the processing entirely
Only changes what you see, while the analysis continues
Deletes previously processed content
items.explain: Hiding is not disabling, and the wording is your only clue.

items.q: Turning off an AI feature usually:
options: Also stops your content being used for training
Leaves training to a separate setting
Deletes your data from the provider
items.explain: You can switch off suggestions and still be contributing text.

items.q: When a feature genuinely cannot be disabled, a legitimate control is:
options: Using a different tool for that content
Accepting it, since nothing can be done
Reporting the vendor
items.explain: Choosing not to use a tool for certain material is a real control, and sometimes the only one available.

items.q: Voice input on a phone is often better than typing because:
options: Recognition is more accurate than keyboards
It is faster and you supply far more context than you would thumb-type
It uses less data
items.explain: Rambling is fine — models handle disfluent speech, and richer context produces better answers.

items.q: On-device processing means the feature:
options: Is more capable than the cloud version
Works offline, costs no data, and transmits nothing
Requires a subscription
items.explain: It is less capable and adequate for a great deal — and it resolves the paste test differently.

items.q: Which mobile cost is most often overlooked?
options: Mobile data used by cloud AI features
The subscription price
Screen wear
items.explain: Battery and storage matter too, and none appears in the feature description.

items.q: Email thread summaries most often lose:
options: The subject line
Conditions, attribution and the actual ask
Participant names
items.explain: "Thursday if the figures arrive by Tuesday" becoming "they agreed to Thursday" is the characteristic failure.

items.q: The real risk of suggested replies is:
options: The English is often wrong
They encourage replying without reading, so you agree to things
They are too formal
items.explain: "Sounds good!" on a message whose second paragraph committed you to a cost is the failure that matters.

items.q: An always-on email summariser involves whose privacy?
options: Only yours, since it is your account
Also your correspondents', who never chose it and cannot object
Nobody's, if the provider does not train on it
items.explain: They wrote to a person, not a processing service — and it matters most in privileged or protected roles.

items.q: Priority sorting fails invisibly because:
options: It runs overnight
You cannot notice the message you were not shown
It does not log its decisions
items.explain: Unlike a bad summary there is no output to inspect — and unusual, atypical messages are what it handles worst.

items.q: The core right in many data protection regimes concerns:
options: Any use of AI by an organisation
Solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects
Only employment decisions
items.explain: The threshold phrase does real work — a recommendation feed is not the same category as a mortgage refusal.

items.q: The fastest route to changing an automated decision is often:
options: Challenging the algorithm's design
Checking and correcting the data it was based on
Reapplying immediately
items.explain: Old addresses, mismatched names and duplicate records are common. Wrong input means re-running, not arguing.

items.q: Requests for human review should be made in writing because:
options: Phone staff cannot help
It starts a formal clock, creates a record, and reaches the team who must answer
Verbal requests are invalid
items.explain: It also lets you be factual and specific, which is what gets a request routed rather than deflected.

items.q: The most common workplace situation regarding AI tooling:
options: A clear policy everyone has read
Confident beliefs with no document behind them
No tools deployed
items.explain: "They can read everything" and "nobody's looking" are both guesses; the policy usually exists and is unread.

items.q: Automatic transcription in a work meeting:
options: Needs no announcement, being a company tool
Still requires everyone to know, and in many places to agree
Only needs announcing to external participants
items.explain: Colleagues are people, and the announcement is what makes it lawful in many jurisdictions.

items.q: When AI-derived metrics feed your performance review, ask:
options: Which model is used
What is measured, whether it captures the job, and whether a person can overrule it
How often it runs
items.explain: Activity metrics reliably miss thinking and mentoring, and a reviewer without authority is worse than none.

items.q: Why re-run a settings audit after a redesign?
options: Settings expire
New features arrive switched on, and migrations sometimes reset preferences
Providers must reset them
items.explain: A tool audited in March can gain a default-on feature in June, announced in a changelog nobody reads.

items.q: If a feature cannot be disabled, the audit still helps because:
options: You can complain more effectively
Knowing what is running lets you decide what to put into it
It may become disableable later
items.explain: The confidential conversation happens elsewhere; the search summary gets checked like any other AI output.
